job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below are the issues I found, in section order. I'm not a substitute for outside counsel, so please have them confirm the legal points, especially items 17, 24, 25 and 29. Items are tagged where they matter most for evasion (E), enforceability (N), or legal challenge (C).

**Section 2 (Definitions)**

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold (E).** The 10,000 t/year test applies to "a single vessel," with no aggregation across a fleet, affiliates, or a joint venture. An operator could run several vessels, each under the threshold, and never trigger the prohibition.

2. **§2(1)(A), "per year" (E, N).** "Year" is undefined (calendar, rolling 12 months, or license year). A short campaign under the threshold, followed by a pause or a vessel swap, may never qualify. It is also unclear on which day a violation occurs when the threshold is crossed mid-year, which complicates the per-day penalty in §5(a).

3. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and units (N, C).** "Recovery" is undefined: it could mean lifting from the seabed, arrival on deck, or processed product. The text doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry weight, and nodules carry significant moisture. Operators can contest the measurement, and prosecutors can't prove it cleanly.

4. **§2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" (C).** Read literally, this covers deepwater oil and gas production, sand and gravel, and other seabed extraction below 200 m, since hydrocarbons are arguably "mineral resources." This overbreadth invites opposition and challenges from other industries and could be used to argue the bill is unworkable.

5. **§2(1)(A), "depths greater than 200 meters" (E, N).** The text doesn't say how depth is measured (datum, point of recovery, or along a mining track that crosses the 200 m line). It also bears no relation to the bill's "deep seabed" title, and it leaves out shallower deposits.

6. **§2(1), no commercial element (N, C).** The definition is volume-based only. A non-commercial or government operation above 10,000 t is "commercial," while a for-profit operation under 10,000 t is not. That mismatch with the defined term is easy to attack.

7. **§2(1)(B), Secretary's determination (N, C).** "The Secretary" is never identified (Commerce, Interior, or State), and "risks comparable to" has no standard. There is no rulemaking, notice, publication, or review requirement, and violations carry criminal penalties. This invites vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges and a rule-of-lenity defense.

8. **§2(2), "U.S. person" (E).** It covers only citizens and corporations organized under State law. It omits LLCs and partnerships (arguably), trusts, permanent residents, entities organized in territories or D.C. ("State" is undefined), and foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies. There is no ownership or control test.

9. **§2(3), "covered vessel" (E, N).** A vessel under 5,000 GT can mine without registering, while a registered vessel over 5,000 GT recovering under 10,000 t isn't prohibited at all, so the registry and the prohibition don't line up. "Equipped for the recovery" is also vague and can be avoided by temporary or modular equipment. The definition misses the collector vehicles, risers, and platforms that do the actual recovery.

10. **Undefined terms throughout (N, C).** "Person," "United States," "State," "operator," "exploration license," and "mining" (used in §3(b) instead of the defined term) are all undefined. Whether "United States" includes the EEZ, the territorial sea, or U.S. territories decides the reach of §3(a).

**Section 3 (Prohibition)**

11. **§3(a), jurisdictional gaps (E).** It reaches only persons "in the United States" and U.S. persons. It has no flag-vessel prong, so a U.S.-flagged vessel owned and operated by a foreign entity at sea is arguably outside it. Foreign companies and foreign-incorporated affiliates of U.S. firms are also outside it.

12. **§3(a), no ancillary conduct covered (E).** It bars only "engaging in" mining. It doesn't reach financing, chartering vessels, importing, processing, buying, or transporting nodules mined by others, or aiding and abetting. U.S. firms could remain involved through offtake agreements, onshore processing, or equity in foreign operators.

13. **§3(a), exploration not prohibited (E).** Exploration is neither banned nor regulated, so firms can continue surveys and sampling and wait for the prohibition to lapse.

14. **§3(b), grandfather clause (E, N).** The exemption covers "mining conducted under" any pre-enactment "exploration license," which could be read to allow commercial-scale recovery. "Exploration license" is undefined, so licenses issued by foreign states or the International Seabed Authority might qualify. There is no volume cap, expiry, or limit on renewal, modification, or transfer to affiliates. It also doesn't say what happens if the license is revoked or lapses.

15. **§3(b), cutoff date creates a rush (E).** The exemption turns on "date of enactment," yet the Act takes effect 180 days later (§8). That gives a window to obtain or amend licenses. Pending applicants, who aren't covered, have strong due process and takings arguments (C).

16. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption (E).** The exemption turns on subjective purpose, with no volume cap, duration limit, permit requirement, or approval by any agency. A large-scale "test" extraction could qualify. It also doesn't bar selling or retaining the recovered material.

17. **Relationship to existing law (N, C).** The bill doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.), which authorizes exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits, and it has no conforming amendments or savings clause. Courts disfavor implied repeal, so holders of existing licenses and permits could argue those authorizations survive, and the conflict will produce litigation.

**Section 4 (Registry)**

18. **§4(a), registration (N).** There is no deadline, no required content, no rulemaking authority, and no definition of "operator" (owner, charterer, or manager). It's also unclear whether foreign-flagged vessels or foreign operators must register.

19. **§4(b), reporting (N).** The quarterly report is "certified by the operator" with no content standard, verification, audit or inspection authority, vessel tracking, or public-release rules. There is no mechanism to check the tonnage figures that the §2(1)(A) threshold depends on.

20. **§4 has no enforcement mechanism (N).** §5 penalizes only violations of §3. Failing to register or report, or filing a false report, carries no penalty under this Act, so the registry is effectively voluntary (beyond whatever general false-statement law applies).

**Section 5 (Penalties)**

21. **§5(a), no enforcement structure (N).** The section doesn't say who assesses penalties, whether through administrative proceedings or Justice Department civil suits. It sets no notice-and-hearing process or penalty factors. It provides no injunctions, vessel or mineral forfeiture, or citizen suits, and no inflation adjustment.

22. **§5(a) vs. §8, retroactivity conflict (N, C).** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act, including §3, doesn't take effect until 180 days later. Conduct in that window is both unlawful and not yet regulated, which is internally contradictory and invites due process and fair-notice challenges.

23. **§5(a), "each day" and size of penalty (N, C).** "Each day on which the violation occurs" is hard to apply to an annual-tonnage violation (see item 2). Up to $1,000,000 per day also invites an Excessive Fines challenge, particularly where the underlying standard is vague.

24. **§5(b), criminal penalty (N, C).** "Willfully" doesn't say what the defendant must know, such as the law, the volume, or the Secretary's §2(1)(B) determination. Combined with the vague definitions, this makes convictions difficult and invites a vagueness challenge. There is also no provision on corporate officer liability.

**Sections 6–8 (Agreement, Duration, Effective Date)**

25. **§6, international agreement (N).** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes no result and no consequence. It has no reporting requirement, funding, definition of "equivalent," or fallback if negotiations fail, so it has no practical effect.

26. **§7(a), repeal trigger (N, C).** The terms "finds by joint resolution" and "without serious harm" are undefined. No one is required to commission or deliver the National Academies report, and no deadline or funding is set. A joint resolution is also subject to veto, and its legal effect is unclear (does it end the prohibition automatically?).

27. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), conflicting duration (N, C).** One provision ends the prohibition on a congressional finding, the other on a fixed 10-year sunset, and the Act doesn't say which governs. The sunset runs from enactment, not the effective date, so the prohibition lasts only about 9.5 years.

28. **§7(b), no savings clause (E, N).** The Act "ceases to have effect" with no provision preserving liability for violations committed before the sunset. Defendants may argue that prosecutions and penalties abate, since the general saving statute (1 U.S.C. §109) addresses repeal and arguably not expiration.

29. **§8, 180-day delay (E).** The delay gives operators six months to ramp up, stockpile, obtain licenses, or begin recovery. The Act has no transition rule for operations that start in that window.

**General omissions**

30. **No severability clause (C).** If a court strikes the §2(1)(B) delegation or the penalty provisions, nothing says the rest survives.

31. **No regulatory or judicial-review provisions (N, C).** The Act has no rulemaking authority, designated lead agency, appropriations, or judicial-review provisions, and it doesn't address takings or compensation for affected investments.

32. **No international-law savings clause (C).** Applying §3(a) to U.S. persons "anywhere" without addressing high-seas freedoms or the U.S. position on UNCLOS invites a legal and diplomatic challenge.

**A note on strategy:** many of these are fixable with a technical amendment, so raising them publicly before Thursday may prompt the sponsors to tighten the text. Items 4, 7, 17, 22, 26 and 27 are the strongest arguments that the bill is poorly drafted without helping its authors close the loopholes (items 1, 3, 8, 11–14, 16 and 29).
